planting.note: Sow seed on the soil surface in fall or very early spring, pressing lightly but leaving exposed to light; a gritty, lean, sharply drained site mimicking rocky Iberian slopes prevents crown rot over winter.

directions: Grow in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in part shade to full sun; Spanish foxglove is a compact, short-lived perennial native to rocky, siliceous slopes of central and western Spain and Portugal, distinct from the taller biennial common foxglove. Downy grey-green leaves set off dense one-sided spikes of rose-pink to purplish-pink tubular flowers marked with darker interior spotting through early to midsummer. Good drainage matters more than fertility for longevity, so avoid heavy, wet clay and rich amended beds where the crown is prone to rot. Established plants self-sow modestly on gravelly or scree plantings, renewing the colony without becoming weedy.

planting.note: Surface-sow in fall or early spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil; like other perennial foxgloves the fine seed needs light and should not be buried.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; native to rocky woodland edges and scrub of the Balkan Peninsula and Turkey, this uncommon perennial foxglove sends up narrow spikes of soft yellowish-green to olive-brown tubular flowers with faint interior veining from early to midsummer, closer in scale and color to Digitalis lutea but taller and slightly larger-flowered. The narrow, glossy foliage forms a tidy basal rosette that persists as a low mound after bloom. It is a genuine perennial rather than a monocarpic biennial, returning reliably for several years where drainage is good, and pairs well with ferns and other woodland-edge perennials that share its subtle, understated coloring. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting, though it self-sows lightly and is never aggressive.

planting.note: Sow seed on the surface in fall or early spring in lean, well-drained soil; this Balkan native persists best where summer moisture is moderate rather than constantly wet.

directions: Grow in lean to average, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; naked-flowered foxglove is native to rocky slopes and open woodland of the Balkan Peninsula, taking its common name from the smooth, glossy, sparingly hairy leaves that distinguish it from the downy foliage of most other foxgloves. One-sided spikes of yellowish-brown tubular flowers etched with a fine maroon net of veining open over a long midsummer season above a neat basal rosette. It behaves as a short-lived perennial or biennial depending on conditions, and light self-sowing on open, gravelly ground keeps a planting going without staking or fuss. A good choice for a dry shade or rock garden border seeking a foxglove with unusual coloring beyond the common pink and white.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring into moist, humus-rich soil; established colonies can be lifted and divided every three to four years to control spread and renew vigor.

directions: Plant in moist to consistently damp, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; 'Superba' is the most widely grown selection of European bistort, an RHS Award of Garden Merit winner valued for its more compact, floriferous habit and larger, brighter rose-pink bottlebrush spikes than the wild species. Bloom is heaviest in early summer, with a reliable scattered rebloom into late summer if spent spikes are sheared back after the first flush. The dense, dock-like foliage spreads steadily by rhizome into a tidy weed-suppressing groundcover, making it well suited to pond margins, moist border edges, and rain gardens where the soil never fully dries out. Because it is a named clone, propagate by division rather than seed to keep the improved flower quality and habit true.
